summary: Describes an interface for importing external pre-shared keys into TLS 1.3. The aim is to let an external key be used safely with the protocol rather than being reused in ways that could cause problems. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: You have a key from a friend and want to use it for different locks. This gives a safe way to bring that key in so it is turned into a fresh, proper key for each lock.

subtitle: How to turn a pre-shared key provisioned outside TLS into separate, safely bound keys for TLS 1.3.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 requires each pre-shared key to be used with a single hash function, but an external key may also be used with TLS 1.2 and other hashes, which can produce related outputs and security problems.
tldr.mechanism: A PSK importer derives a distinct key and identity for each target protocol and key derivation function, mixing in an optional context string, and changes the binder key label to "imp binder".
tldr.outcome: Each imported key is used with one KDF at most and cannot be confused with a non-imported PSK, though the RFC still advises provisioning separate PSKs for TLS 1.3 and earlier versions.

today: RFC 9258 is a Proposed Standard from July 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147).

sections.title: Why External PSKs Need Importing
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) supports Pre-Shared Key (PSK) authentication. A PSK can come from a session ticket of an earlier connection, or from an external, out-of-band mechanism. The protocol mandates that each PSK be used with a single hash function, which simplifies protocol analysis. TLS 1.2 has no such rule: a PSK can be used with any hash algorithm and the TLS 1.2 pseudorandom function.

There is no known way that the same external PSK produces related output in TLS 1.3 and earlier versions, but only limited analysis has been done. Applications SHOULD provision separate PSKs for (D)TLS 1.3 and prior versions. Where that is not possible, such as already-deployed PSKs, reuse may produce related outputs and lead to security problems.

To mitigate this, RFC 9258 specifies a PSK importer interface. It binds an external PSK to a specific key derivation function (KDF) and hash function for TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147). One PSK and identity expand into a set of PSKs and identities.
sections.plainLanguage: One shared secret is risky if you use it in many different places. The importer makes a fresh copy of the secret for each place, so the copies stay apart.

sections.title: Terms Used by the Importer
sections.content:
An External PSK (EPSK) is a PSK provisioned out of band. It is a tuple of Base Key, External Identity and Hash. The Base Key is the secret value, and the External Identity is a byte sequence that identifies the EPSK.

The target protocol and target KDF are the protocol and KDF for which a PSK is imported. An Imported PSK (IPSK) is a TLS PSK derived from an EPSK, an optional context string, a target protocol and a target KDF. Its identifier is the Imported Identity. A non-imported PSK is an EPSK used directly as a TLS PSK.
sections.plainLanguage: The original secret is the master copy. An imported key is a copy made for one particular lock, with its own label.

sections.title: How the Importer Works in Outline
sections.content:
The importer mirrors the TLS exporter interface in that it diversifies a key from contextual information. It takes an external PSK and identity and creates a set of derived PSKs and identities that are each unique. Each is bound to a target protocol, a KDF identifier and an optional context string. The PSK binder keys also get a new derivation label, so imported and non-imported PSKs cannot be confused.

Imported keys need no negotiation: a client and server will not agree on identities if the import was done incorrectly. Endpoints can deploy importer support step by step by offering non-imported PSKs for TLS versions before 1.3. Imported and non-imported PSKs are not equivalent because their identities differ.

Endpoints that import keys MUST NOT use the input keys for anything other than the importer, and MUST NOT use the derived keys for anything other than TLS PSKs. Each external PSK fed to the importer MUST be associated with at most one hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: Every copy of the key gets its own name tag, so the two sides only match up if they both made the copy the same way.

sections.title: The ImportedIdentity and Key Derivation
sections.content:
For each supported target protocol and KDF the importer builds an ImportedIdentity structure containing external_identity, context, target_protocol and target_kdf (a 16-bit value). External PSKs MUST NOT be imported for (D)TLS 1.2 or earlier. The context MUST include the context used to determine the EPSK, if any, and MUST include a channel binding for the deriving protocols. The target_protocol is the (D)TLS version; TLS 1.3 uses 0x0304, which QUICv1 therefore also uses.

The imported key is computed in two steps: epskx = HKDF-Extract(0, epsk), then ipskx = HKDF-Expand-Label(epskx, "derived psk", Hash(ImportedIdentity), L). L is the output length of the target KDF, for example 32 octets for SHA256. The HKDF hash is the one associated with the EPSK, and SHA-256 SHOULD be used if there is none.

The serialized ImportedIdentity is sent as PskIdentity.identity in the PSK extension. Because that extension is limited to 2^16 - 1 octets, the interface SHOULD reject an ImportedIdentity that is larger. Endpoints SHOULD generate a key for each target ciphersuite they offer: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 need two keys, while TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 need only one.

EPSKs MAY be imported before a connection starts if targets and contexts are known, and MAY be imported for early data if they are bound to the required settings, such as the ALPN value and QUIC transport parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe mixes the secret with a label that says which lock it is for and who is using it. A different label gives a completely different key.

sections.title: The Binder Key Label
sections.content:
In the standard TLS 1.3 key schedule, the binder key is derived from the Early Secret with the label "ext binder" or "res binder". Imported PSKs use the label "imp binder" instead.

This ensures a client and server negotiate use of an external PSK if and only if both endpoints import it or neither does. Because the binder key is a leaf key, changing its computation does not affect any other key.

To retire a hash function, an endpoint removes the matching KDF from its set of target KDFs. This does not change the KDF operation used to derive imported PSKs.
sections.plainLanguage: Imported keys get a special stamp. If one side stamps the key and the other does not, the stamps do not match and the door stays shut.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
Deployments that already use a PSK with TLS 1.2 would, when adding the importer, use that same key both directly as a TLS 1.2 PSK and as an EPSK. The same KDF and key would then be used in two protocol contexts. This is not a recommended configuration.

The benefits of TLS 1.3 and importers may still be compelling enough that existing deployments choose this noncompliant setup for a brief transition period while new software is rolled out. Operators are advised to make any such period as short as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: If you must use the same key in the old and new systems for a while, do it only briefly and then stop.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security goal is to avoid PSK reuse across KDFs while properly authenticating endpoints. The RFC states four goals: imported PSKs achieve compound authentication of the provisioning process and the connection; context-free PSKs authenticate only within a single connection; imported PSKs are not used as input to two different KDFs; and they do not collide with future protocol versions and KDFs.

The importer does not stop applications from building non-importer identities that collide with imported identities. Appendix A covers the Selfie reflection attack, which arises when several nodes share one PSK: a node can end up authenticating itself. Putting both peers' roles into the context string, for example client and server MAC addresses, makes the handshake fail if a ClientHello is redirected.

On privacy, external PSK identities are often static and may become a persistent tracking identifier. The context is visible in cleartext on the wire, so applications SHOULD NOT put sensitive information there unless protected, for example by Encrypted Client Hello.
sections.plainLanguage: Each copy of the key can only open one lock, and the label on it is visible to everyone, so do not write secrets on the label.

sections.title: The TLS KDF Identifiers Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the "TLS KDF Identifiers" registry. Value 0x0000 is Reserved, 0x0001 is HKDF_SHA256 and 0x0002 is HKDF_SHA384.

New values in the range 0x0000 to 0xfeff are assigned by Specification Required. The range 0xff00 to 0xffff is reserved for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list that gives each key-making method its own number, with some numbers set aside for private use.
